title: How Janitorial Workers' Comp Class Codes (9014 & 9015) Affect In-House Employer Payroll
seoTitle: Janitorial Workers' Comp Class Codes (9014 vs. 9015) Payroll Guide
metaDescription: Janitorial workers' comp class codes 9014 and 9015 add $3.50-$8.20 per $100 of W-2 payroll. Compare in-house vs. vendor COI risk in our Calculator.
excerpt: Hiring an in-house W-2 custodian triggers a mandatory reclassification under NCCI workers' compensation class codes 9014 or 9015, multiplying your insurance premium by 25x to 45x compared to clerical office staff. Learn how loss-cost multipliers, Experience Modification Rates (EMR), and ergonomic equipment reduce your payroll burden.
quickAnswer: In-house commercial janitors are classified under NCCI workers' comp class codes 9014 (Janitorial Services by Contractors) or 9015 (Buildings—Operation by Owner or Lessee), carrying national average base rates of $3.50 to $8.20 per $100 of gross W-2 payroll—compared to just $0.10 to $0.22 per $100 for Clerical Office Employees (Class 8810). For a full-time custodian earning $41,600 annually ($20/hour), workers' compensation insurance alone adds $1,456 to $3,411 per year ($121–$284/month) before factoring in Experience Modification Rate (EMR) penalties from slip-and-fall or lifting claims.

blocks.text: The Hidden Payroll Shock: Clerical Code 8810 vs. Janitorial Codes 9014 and 9015

When a software company, law firm, medical practice, or corporate regional office decides to bring office cleaning in-house by hiring a W-2 janitor, the finance team often models payroll expenses using the company's existing corporate fringe rate. Because 95% of white-collar office employees fall under National Council on Compensation Insurance (NCCI) Class Code 8810 (Clerical Office Employees), the employer is accustomed to paying a negligible $0.10 to $0.22 per $100 of payroll for workers' compensation coverage.

However, workers comp class codes are assigned by the specific physical exposure of the employee's duties—and at your annual workers' compensation premium audit, the insurance carrier's auditor will inspect W-2 job descriptions and payroll registers. The moment an employee pushes a vacuum, mops a ceramic tile restroom floor, carries 33-gallon trash bags to a loading dock, or mixes chemical concentrates, their entire gross wage is reclassified into building maintenance or janitorial hazard brackets that cost 25 to 45 times more per dollar of payroll.

Understanding how underwriters distinguish between NCCI Class Code 9015, NCCI Class Code 9014, and state-specific bureaus (such as California WCIRB, New York NYCIRB, or Pennsylvania PCRB) is essential before deciding between an in-house custodian and an outsourced janitorial service.
NCCI & State Bureau Rate Benchmarks by Workers' Comp Class Code

Across the 38 states governed directly by NCCI—as well as independent rating bureau states—custodial and facility maintenance personnel fall into four primary classifications. The table below outlines the typical rate range per $100 of gross W-2 payroll, annual premium per full-time custodian ($41,600 base wage at $20/hour across 2,080 annual hours), and the operational triggers for each code.

blocks.title: The 'Single Enterprise / No Payroll Division' Audit Trap
blocks.text: Under NCCI Basic Manual Rule 1-D-3, an individual employee's payroll cannot be split between Clerical (Code 8810) and Building Operation/Janitorial (Code 9015). If you pay a $52,000/year office coordinator to spend 30 hours a week at the reception desk and 10 hours a week vacuuming and cleaning restrooms, the insurance auditor will reclassify 100% of their $52,000 salary into Code 9015—triggering an unexpected $2,300+ audit bill.
How One Custodial Injury Impacts Your Corporate Experience Modification Rate (EMR)

For mid-sized and enterprise employers, the direct premium of $1,456 to $2,662 per custodian under Class Code 9015 is only half of the financial risk. The larger exposure lies in your company's Experience Modification Rate (EMR or 'Mod Factor'). An EMR of 1.00 represents the industry average; a clean loss history can drop your EMR to 0.75 (a 25% discount across your entire corporate policy), whereas workplace injury claims can push your EMR to 1.25 or 1.45 for three consecutive policy years.

Commercial janitorial work carries one of the highest frequencies of musculoskeletal sprains, rotator cuff tears, lower-back disc injuries from hoisting wet trash liners, and slip-and-fall injuries on freshly mopped ceramic tile (1.12x labor multiplier) or VCT floors (1.04x multiplier). According to National Safety Council workers' compensation claim benchmarks, the average lost-time strain or fall claim costs $32,000 to $48,000 in combined medical payments and temporary total disability (TTD) indemnity wages.

If an in-house W-2 janitor suffers a $40,000 lower-back injury lifting heavy waste barrels or slipping in a restroom, the resulting 0.18 to 0.25 jump in your corporate EMR does not just raise the janitor's premium—it multiplies the workers' compensation premium across your entire company's payroll (including sales, engineering, warehouse, and executive staff) for the next 36 months. When you outsource cleaning to a qualified janitorial contractor ($35 to $65/hour or $0.05 to $0.15/sq ft), every injury claim stays on the contractor's policy and their EMR.
Ergonomic Equipment Capex That Lowers In-House Janitorial Claim Frequency

If your facility retains in-house W-2 custodians or daytime porters under Class Code 9015, underwriters and loss-control engineers look closely at your mechanical ergonomics program. Overexertion from pushing heavy, clogged residential vacuums across commercial glue-down carpet tiles or bending repeatedly to unjam brushrolls accounts for more than 35% of custodial workers' comp claims. Equipping in-house staff with lightweight, commercial-grade upright vacuums reduces physical fatigue and repetitive-motion claims:

items: Low-Strain Lightweight Daily Vacuuming: The Hoover Commercial TaskVac CH53010 Lightweight Upright weighs just 15 pounds with a 13-inch cleaning path, a 3.7-quart top-fill HEPA bag, and a 35-foot quick-change power cord that lets custodians cover large open office zones without constant stooping to unplug and replug cords.

Metal-Debris Protection Without Manual Brush Clearing: The Bissell Commercial BG101DC Dirt Cup Upright Vacuum incorporates a front magnet bar ahead of its 12-inch steel brushroll to catch staples and paper clips before they jam the belt, reducing laceration and wrist-strain hazards during maintenance, paired with a clear dirt cup and washable filter.

Dual-Motor Ergonomics with Onboard Reach Wand: For custodians detailing cubicle walls and baseboard crevices, the ProTeam ProForce 1500XP HEPA Upright Vacuum pairs a 15-inch floor path and 3.25-quart HEPA media filtration at 67 dBA with an instant-release onboard wand so staff never have to haul a separate canister or bend on their knees.

blocks.text: 4-Step Audit Protocol to Protect Your Facility from Workers' Comp Liability

items.name: Segregate W-2 Custodial Payroll from Clerical Staff
items.text: Never assign part-time janitorial duties to front-desk receptionists or administrative assistants coded under 8810. Keep all physical cleaning strictly confined to dedicated W-2 custodians coded under 9015 or transfer the scope to an outsourced contractor.

items.name: Prohibit High-Elevation Exterior Window Work (Avoid Code 9170)
items.text: Include a strict written rule in your in-house custodian's job description prohibiting ladder work above 6 feet or any exterior window washing above the ground floor. This prevents auditors from bumping your payroll into high-risk Code 9170 ($9.50–$18.40 per $100).

items.name: Enforce Strict Certificate of Insurance (COI) Waivers on Outsourced Vendors
items.text: If you outsource cleaning to transfer workers' comp risk, verify that the contractor holds an active statutory Workers' Compensation policy in your state with a Waiver of Subrogation endorsement before they set foot on site. Under uninsured subcontractor laws in almost every US state, if an uninsured janitorial vendor's worker is injured in your office, your company's workers' comp policy must pay the claim.

items.name: Institute Written OSHA HazCom & Slip-Resistant Footwear Rules
items.text: Provide employer-paid ASTM F2913 slip-resistant footwear ($65–$110/year per custodian), wheeled brute dollies for trash barrels, and closed-loop chemical dispensers compliant with OSHA 29 CFR 1910.1200 to Qualify for state safety-credit discounts (typically 2% to 5% off workers' comp premiums).

faqs.q: What is the difference between Workers' Comp Class Code 9014 and Class Code 9015?
faqs.a: NCCI Class Code 9014 applies to third-party janitorial contractors whose business is cleaning client buildings for a fee. NCCI Class Code 9015 (Buildings—Operation by Owner or Lessee) applies when a property owner or commercial office tenant hires their own in-house W-2 janitors, day porters, or facility maintenance staff to care for their own occupied space. Code 9015 typically carries a 15% to 25% lower base rate than Code 9014 because in-house staff work in a familiar, single-site environment.

faqs.q: Can I avoid workers' comp insurance by hiring an independent cleaner on a 1099 form?
faqs.a: No. Paying a solo cleaner via 1099-NEC without verifying their own active Workers' Compensation Certificate of Insurance is one of the costliest mistakes an office manager can make. At your annual insurance audit, your carrier will automatically add 100% of payments made to uninsured 1099 cleaners straight onto your policy under Class Code 9014—and if that 1099 cleaner is injured on your floors, your company is legally liable as the statutory employer.

faqs.q: How do state monopolistic workers' comp funds handle janitorial class codes?
faqs.a: Four US states—Ohio, Washington, Wyoming, and North Dakota—operate monopolistic state workers' compensation funds where employers must purchase coverage directly from the state agency rather than private carriers. For example, Washington L&I classifies building janitors by experience hours rather than per-$100 of payroll, making loss prevention and light-duty return-to-work programs even more critical for controlling hourly premium assessments.

faqs.q: Does switching to a 3x/week outsourced janitorial crew completely eliminate our Code 9015 exposure?
faqs.a: Yes, provided the outsourced janitorial company carries statutory Workers' Compensation coverage verified via an active COI directly from their insurer, and none of your internal W-2 office staff perform physical janitorial or building maintenance duties.
